Meir (Meirel) Lifshitz, son of Rivka and Menahem, was born on the sixth day of Nisan 5683 (23 March 1923) in the town of Stashov, Poland. In his parents' home he was raised in a traditional Jewish manner and in the spirit of Zionism, in preparation for pioneering agricultural life. He studied in a *heder* (traditional Jewish primary school) and then in a elementary school. At the age of 16 he completed elementary school and was about to emigrate to Eretz Israel to join the youth village of Ben Shemen, but while he was in Vilna, preparing for a training course, the Second World War broke out and he was forced to return to his parents' home. He volunteered for forced labor for the Germans in place of his father and brother, and was taken to an extermination camp. Only the hope of reaching Eretz Israel strengthened his spirit through all the hardships he endured. He wandered from one concentration camp to another: in Poland (Skarżysko-Kamienna) and in Germany (Buchenwald, Schlieben, Theresienstadt). In Landsberg, Germany, he met his brother, who had arrived from Eretz Israel with the Jewish Brigade, and with his brother's help he emigrated to Eretz Israel aboard the illegal immigrant ship *Tel Hai* on 28 March 1946. After spending two weeks in the Atlit detention camp, he went to kibbutz Masada, and from there to kibbutz Kfar HaHoresh. In 1947 his father arrived in Eretz Israel, and Meir left the kibbutz in order to help him. His devotion to his father was exemplary. Meir was a dark-eyed young man of strong character and a generous spirit. Through all the suffering he endured, he knew how to keep his emotional balance.

From the beginning of his time in the country he was a member of the Haganah. In early 1948 he enlisted and served in one of the battalions of the Carmeli Brigade. He was the only one left of the family's six children (a sister and three brothers were murdered by the Nazis, and another brother, Isaac, fell at Rmat Naftali), but his father was unable to have him released on the grounds that he was an only son. Meir took part in the conquest of Haifa and Acre, and from there he was sent to the Upper Galilee, to help the besieged settlements, and arrived at the place where his brother had fallen. On the third day of Sivan 5708 (10 June 1948), the day before the first truce began, he fell in the battle for Rmat Naftali. He was laid to rest in the cemetery at Rmat Naftali, beside the grave of his brother Isaac, who had fallen four weeks earlier.
